# Preface {#sec-about .unnumbered}

## Who This Book Is For {#sec-book-audience .unlisted}

This textbook is written for computer science and electrical engineering students, machine learning systems researchers, and systems architects who are crossing the chasm from digital machine learning into physical artificial intelligence. The primary reader understands modern computing systems: GPU and NPU accelerator architectures, high-bandwidth memory hierarchies, distributed collective communications, PyTorch and JAX computational graphs, custom Triton and CUDA kernels, KV-cache paging, and operating system concurrency.

In digital machine learning systems—the domain of large language models, recommendation engines, and multimodal advisory services explored in the earlier volumes of this curriculum—computation operates in a forgiving digital environment. Hardware is treated as an abstract, infinitely compliant execution engine. Compute substrates sit in climate-controlled server racks where power distribution networks maintain stable rail voltages across transient load spikes, memory management units provide virtual memory isolation, and hardware faults are masked by error-correcting codes. An out-of-bounds array access raises an exception, an erroneous prediction is caught by application logic, and a failed inference request costs only a recomputed activation or a discarded token. Digital state transitions are fully reversible: database transactions support atomic rollback, distributed training frameworks reload checkpoints from distributed object stores after an accelerator node fails, and network layers retransmit dropped packets. Execution models leverage speculative execution, memory overcommitment, out-of-order execution, and dynamic garbage collection. Under these forgiving assumptions, the primary systems objective is throughput: packing tokens into massive batches ($B \gg 1$), saturating systolic tensor arrays, overlapping communication with computation, and maximizing arithmetic intensity under memory bandwidth limits governed by the classical Roofline model ($y = \min(\text{Peak FLOP/s}, \text{Peak BW} \times I)$).

Physical AI terminates that digital forgiveness. Physical artificial intelligence begins where computation ceases to be symbolic and becomes physical force. When a vision-language-action model commands an autonomous mobile robot or an articulated manipulator, execution crosses the causal boundary into continuous Newtonian physics. Software directs matter, momentum, and energy. When an algorithm drives a brushless permanent-magnet motor through a pulse-width modulated (PWM) inverter, software manipulates electromagnetic fields that drive stator coils, accelerate rotor mass, and transmit mechanical torque through precision gearboxes.

Newtonian physics provides no pause mechanism. Continuous physical time marches forward regardless of whether a software thread is executing, stalled on memory bus crossbar contention, or blocked on garbage collection. Once a 50 kg mobile base accelerates to an aisle cruising speed of $v = 1.3\text{ m/s}$, the plant possesses over $42\text{ J}$ of kinetic energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$), and an articulated arm swinging a payload possesses substantial angular momentum ($L = I\omega$). Newtonian momentum admits no pause button: that kinetic energy cannot be discarded, garbage-collected, or rolled back. It must be mechanically dissipated through tire-floor Coulomb friction or regenerative braking over a nonzero physical stopping distance:
$$d_{\text{stop}} \approx v \tau_{\text{delay}} + \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{brake}}}$$

In this physical reality, delay is not an interactive inconvenience; delay is distance traveled toward an obstacle. In digital systems, a latency tail spike simply delays time-to-first-token by a few milliseconds. In physical embodiment, every millisecond of latency between photon arrival on an optical sensor and the mechanical application of braking torque ($\tau_{\text{delay}}$)—spent in sensor rolling-shutter exposure, SerDes serialization, PCIe direct memory access (DMA) transfers, neural inference, inter-process communication mailboxes, fieldbus transport (CAN-FD or EtherCAT), microcontroller timer jitter, inverter gate-driver rise time, and motor inductive lag ($L/R$)—translates directly and deterministically into unguided physical displacement ($v \tau_{\text{delay}}$) toward whatever lies ahead.

Furthermore, physical state transitions are thermodynamically and mechanically irreversible:

* **Phase currents and thermal limits**: Every ampere traversing a motor phase winding dissipates irreversible Joule heat ($P = I_{\text{phase}}^2 R_{\text{phase}}$). Rapid cyclic torque reversals dump heat into motor windings whose thermal capacitance and winding-to-housing thermal resistance ($R_{\text{th}}, C_{\text{th}}$) set strict thermal limits. If an unvalidated action chunk commands torque reversals faster than the thermal dissipation envelope of the motor laminations allows, or exceeds the junction temperature of the power silicon, insulation breaks down and phase drivers burn out permanently.
* **Power delivery network droop**: Commanded torque surges draw rapid current transients ($di/dt$) through power distribution cables. Across parasitic harness inductance ($L_{\text{cable}}$), this transient current induces inductive voltage droop ($V_{\text{sag}} = L_{\text{cable}} \frac{di}{dt}$) on DC power rails, which can trip microcontroller undervoltage lockouts (UVLO) and precipitate an unrecoverable system crash.
* **Reflected rotor inertia and non-backdrivable gearboxes**: When commanding articulated joints, torque transmits through high-reduction gearboxes (such as harmonic drives and cycloidal reducers with ratios $N \in [50, 160]$). Because reflected rotor inertia scales quadratically with the reduction ratio ($J_{\text{ref}} = N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}$), the motor rotor appears thousands of times heavier to external impacts. As a result, the transmission is effectively non-backdrivable under high-frequency contact. When an arm strikes a rigid obstacle, the impact energy cannot be absorbed by backdriving the motor; instead, the shock force transmits directly into the flexible spline or gear teeth, causing catastrophic tooth shear unless closed-loop sensing and torque regulation intervene within sub-millisecond physical deadlines.

Once kinetic energy is released, Coulomb friction dissipates heat, or mechanical material yields, software cannot issue an undo, reload a checkpoint, or execute an exception handler.

Because physical reality admits no software rollbacks, physical AI is fundamentally an architectural discipline, not a statistical scaling game. In digital machine learning, empirical scaling laws demonstrate that expanding parameter counts, pretraining tokens, and compute FLOPs predictably drives down cross-entropy validation loss and broadens high-level semantic generalization. In physical systems, however, statistical scaling cannot solve physical dependability for three fundamental reasons:

1. **Average-case empirical risk minimization vs. worst-case physical tail catastrophe**: Deep neural networks are stochastic function approximators trained via empirical risk minimization to optimize expected loss over a distribution: $\min_\theta \mathbb{E}_{(s, a) \sim \mathcal{D}}[L(a, \pi_\theta(s))]$. Even if statistical scaling drives benchmark accuracy to 99.99 percent, a residual failure rate of $10^{-4}$ means an embodied agent running a 50 Hz control loop encounters an unhandled, out-of-distribution failure every three minutes. In digital search or conversational assistants, a $10^{-4}$ error is an unnoticeable formatting glitch or a retried query; in physical embodiment, it is an uncontrolled high-speed collision, an overturned chassis, or a crushed human limb. Physical safety is a worst-case tail phenomenon that average-case statistical optimization cannot bound.
2. **Endogenous closed-loop causality vs. exogenous static datasets**: In digital machine learning, input data distributions are static and exogenous; misclassifying a token or an image does not alter the remaining test examples. In physical AI, actions directly alter future sensory observations through closed-loop plant dynamics ($s_{t+1} \sim P(s \mid s_t, a_t)$). A minor policy execution error displaces the robot into an unfamiliar physical configuration, exposing onboard sensors to out-of-distribution observations that induce further errors. Under this endogenous feedback loop, imitation learning errors compound quadratically over the planning horizon ($\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$, @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws), precipitating sudden policy collapse that static offline pretraining cannot prevent.
3. **Inviolable physical conservation laws vs. unconstrained function approximation**: No volume of training tokens, parameter scaling, or compute can alter Newton's second law ($F = ma$), the conservation of energy, motor back-EMF, or Coulomb friction limits. When an autonomous mobile robot encounters a sudden path intrusion, a hundred-billion-parameter vision-language-action model cannot stop the chassis faster than the tire-ground friction coefficient ($\mu g$) allows, nor can it command motor torque beyond the magnetic saturation limit of the rotor laminations without burning copper. Physical mechanics and thermal limits are non-negotiable physical constraints, not statistical preferences.

Surviving this reality demands an explicit systems architecture that isolates uncertified statistical proposals from deterministic physical execution. The machine cannot be organized as a monolithic neural end-to-end policy. Instead, it must be architecturally partitioned: high-capacity neural networks act strictly as unprivileged proposers in the cognitive Brain, while an independent, deterministic permission path in the Nervous System—evaluated on isolated real-time silicon—validates, bounds, or modifies every command before it crosses the causal boundary into physical force.

Readers approach this architectural challenge from three primary directions:

* **Machine Learning Systems Engineers and Researchers**: Moving beyond open-loop benchmark evaluation on static offline datasets. In physical AI, actions alter future sensory observations through closed-loop feedback ($s_{t+1} \sim P(s \mid s_t, a_t)$), exposing policies to compounding error drift whose worst-case cost scales quadratically with the horizon ($\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$, @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws). ML systems engineers learn why batch throughput must yield to worst-case tail latency, why batch sizes at inference collapse strictly to $B=1$ across time, how to formulate continuous action spaces and trajectory chunks, and how to structure learned models as unprivileged proposers whose outputs must be validated by an independent permission path.
* **Robotics and Control Engineers**: Augmenting classical feedback loops with high-capacity foundation models. Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide open-vocabulary semantic scene understanding and multimodal generalization, but they are stochastic, multi-modal proposers that run at tens of hertz with variable execution latency. Control engineers learn how to interface these learned proposers with deterministic safety filters, such as Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) evaluated as real-time quadratic programs on dedicated safety silicon, ensuring physical invariants remain unbroken.
* **Embedded Systems and Silicon Architects**: Managing multi-rate execution across heterogeneous system-on-chip (SoC) platforms. In physical AI, high-throughput neural processing units share silicon crossbars with deterministic real-time microcontrollers. Architects learn how to isolate safety-critical control loops from accelerator memory traffic, preventing memory bus crossbar contention, DMA starvation, and supply voltage droop from breaching hard real-time physical deadlines.

## Why a Physical AI Systems Textbook {#sec-book-why-physical .unlisted}

This book approaches physical AI from a first-principles systems perspective. Its scope is clearest beside the three neighboring kinds of book that it is not:

* **Not a classical control theory book**: We do not develop continuous-time Laplace transforms, contour integrals, or Lyapunov stability proofs at length. Formal continuous-control proofs and reachability derivations are collected in the volume appendices for optional depth.
* **Not a traditional robotics kinematics book**: We do not work through Denavit-Hartenberg parameter matrices, forward-kinematics linkage catalogs, or specialized mechanical design heuristics.
* **Not an abstract deep learning theory book**: We do not survey loss surface geometry, generalization bounds, or speculative optimizer convergence proofs.

Instead, we reason from physical principles (conservation of energy and momentum, stopping kinematics, thermal dissipation, and Coulomb friction) and from computational systems architecture (multi-rate execution loops, memory bus crossbar contention, asynchronous message queues, and permission paths that check learned proposals).

### Mechanisms taught to the depth that changes a budget

This book does not treat learned models or control blocks as black boxes, and it does not survey their internals either. A mechanism enters the main text at the depth at which it changes a number the machine must budget: a latency, a memory footprint, an energy dissipation ceiling, a spatial clearance, or the evidence a safety claim can rest on. An action-chunk decoder appears through the predictive horizon it supplies and the latency a new chunk takes to generate. A spatial scene representation appears through the memory bandwidth it consumes and the age of the evidence it retains. A barrier filter appears through the mathematical premises its invariance guarantee requires and the real-time deadline it must meet. Algorithmic internals that move no such number—such as the arithmetic of patch tokenization, decoder loss formulations, and surface-reconstruction heuristics—are placed in the appendices for readers who want them.

### Delay is distance

A machine continues moving while it senses, decides, and waits for its brakes. Every millisecond between an observation and the moment braking force builds is spent as physical travel toward whatever the machine must not reach. Consequently, operating speed, computational delay, sensor exposure, actuator time constants, spatial clearance, and braking capacity form a single, coupled physical budget rather than isolated software specifications. The book builds that budget systematically for one machine, adding each term in the chapter that governs it, beginning with the body's stopping distance in @sec-body-kinetic-momentum. A learned model's inference latency enters the budget through the age of the evidence it hands forward, because the permission path, not the neural model, decides at every control tick whether motion may continue.

### From the digital roofline to the physical roofline

In digital machine learning systems, the practitioner's primary performance framework is the Roofline model: compute throughput is bounded by peak arithmetic intensity ($I = \text{FLOPs} / \text{Byte}$) and memory bandwidth. In physical AI, that computational ceiling is merely one link in a larger, coupled **Physical Roofline**. The machine's physical throughput is strictly bounded by:

* **Actuator torque saturation**: Peak joint torque ($\tau_{\max} = k_t I_{\max}$) is bounded by magnetic flux saturation in rotor laminations.
* **Thermal dissipation envelopes**: Continuous torque is limited by irreversible Joule dissipation ($P_{\text{loss}} = I_{\text{phase}}^2 R_{\text{phase}}$), winding thermal resistance ($R_{\text{th}}$), and stator heat dissipation.
* **Power rail inductive droop**: Rapid torque transients command steep current steps ($di/dt$), inducing supply voltage sag ($V_{\text{sag}} = L_{\text{cable}} \frac{di}{dt}$) that bounds peak acceleration.
* **Reflected rotor inertia**: Joint acceleration is bounded by reflected inertia ($J_{\text{ref}} = N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}$) in high-ratio gearboxes, limiting reactive disturbance rejection.
* **Friction and traction limits**: Vehicle deceleration is bounded by tire-floor or foot-ground Coulomb friction ($a_{\max} = \mu g$).
* **End-to-end latency envelopes**: Maximum safe operational velocity is governed by the stopping distance budget: $v_{\max} \le \sqrt{2 a_{\text{brake}} (D_{\text{clear}} - v \tau_{\text{delay}})}$, where $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ integrates sensor exposure, DMA transfer, neural inference, fieldbus transit, and inverter rise time.

Optimizing a physical AI system therefore requires co-designing computational runtimes with mechanical and electrical ceilings: accelerating neural inference FLOPs yields zero physical benefit if the motor inverter is thermally saturated or if braking capacity cannot dissipate the machine's momentum.

## What This Book Promises {#sec-book-promise .unlisted}

This book does not promise a machine that is provably safe. No finite test campaign, runtime safety filter, or certification scheme delivers an absolute safety proof for a learned system in an open world, and each chapter explicitly identifies where guarantees end.

The book teaches something narrower, more rigorous, and achievable. It shows how to architect a machine whose learned proposals cannot authorize their own motion, whose permission path decides on evidence of known age within the physical margins that delay has not yet consumed, and whose every guarantee is documented with the exact premises it rests on. A Control Barrier Function protects the plant only while its dynamic model, state estimation error bounds, actuator authority, and computation deadlines hold. An operational release is justified only for the specific environmental and operational conditions its evidence covers. A premise that physical evidence cannot settle restricts what the machine is permitted to do, rather than being assumed away. The concluding chapter returns to the opening question with this answer: safety guarantees in physical AI are conditional, and the systems engineering discipline lies in determining those conditions, enforcing them in hardware and software, and recording their boundaries in accountable limit records and residual-claims registers.

## The Machine in Five Levels {#sec-book-mental-model .unlisted}

The machine in this book is organized into five levels:

1. The **Brain** holds the learned proposers: multi-modal vision-language-action foundation models and generative diffusion or flow-matching decoders running on high-throughput accelerator silicon (NPUs/GPUs). It revises high-level semantic intent at 1–5 Hz and emits predictive action chunks at 10–30 Hz.
2. Below the **proposal boundary**—the strict architectural demarcation isolating untrusted statistical proposals from physical authority—the **Nervous System** holds the deterministic permission path. Operating on isolated real-time safety silicon (such as lockstep microcontrollers), it evaluates Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) via convex quadratic programming at 100–500 Hz on fresh state evidence, admits, projects, or refuses every proposal, and owns the deterministic emergency fallback.
3. The **Body** is the physical plant under its motor drives: brushless permanent-magnet synchronous motors (PMSM), high-reduction non-backdrivable gearboxes, articulated linkages, mobile chassis, battery packs, and thermal cooling loops.
4. The **Boundary** is where digital bits become physical electromagnetic force and physical phenomena become digital measurements: three-phase inverter gate drivers, analog-to-digital converters (ADCs), optical encoders, inertial measurement units (IMUs), camera SerDes links, and PCIe DMA channels.
5. The **World** comprises everything the machine does not own: terrain, tire-floor Coulomb friction interfaces, dynamic obstacles, ambient illumination shifts, and human coworkers.

Surrounding all five levels is **Governance** as a lifecycle envelope, deciding who may command the machine, how authority transfers between humans and algorithms, and what empirical evidence in limit records and residual-claims registers licenses the system to operate. The Brain proposes; only the permission path permits. @Sec-boundary-machine-model develops the full architectural model and its execution cadences.

## The Three Machine Classes {#sec-book-archetypes .unlisted}

To keep systems concepts concrete, this textbook grounds its principles in the three machine classes of @sec-boundary-three-classes:

1. **Class 1 · Mass-Dominated Mobility (AMRs and Quadrupeds)**: Planar transport bases and legged platforms navigating open facilities and rugged terrain. Governed by vehicle momentum, tire-road and foot-ground Coulomb friction, kinematic stopping distance envelopes, and multi-camera and lidar perception pipelines under rolling-shutter skew.
2. **Class 2 · Contact-Dominated Manipulation**: Multi-link robotic arms and articulated effectors performing dexterous contact tasks. Governed by multi-body rigid dynamics, reflected rotor inertia ($J_{\text{ref}} = N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}$), cycloidal and harmonic gearbox compliance, and contact force containment.
3. **Class 3 · Flow-Dominated Process and Energy Systems**: High-pressure fluid loops, chemical batch reactors, and thermal plants. Governed by enthalpy exchange, pipe fluid dynamics, pressure transients, and irreversible thermodynamic phase changes.

One machine runs through the book, the warehouse mobile manipulator of @sec-boundary-three-classes, and each chapter adds what it owns to that machine's budgets. Each part closes by testing its law on a humanoid, which couples all three classes on one chassis.

## How to Read This Book: Progressive Arc vs. Modular Drop-In {#sec-book-structure .unlisted}

This textbook supports two reading patterns:

### For sequential readers (the cumulative curriculum arc)

Readers moving cover-to-cover follow an introduction, four parts, and a conclusion, and each part is led by one of the book's four laws. @Sec-boundary-book-architecture traces the chain of records the chapters hand forward.

* **Introduction** (@sec-boundary) asks what a machine must guarantee before a learned model's proposal becomes physical work.
* **Part I: The Machine Anatomy** (@sec-body, @sec-brain, @sec-nervous) turns the first law, irreversibility, into budgets of time, distance, torque, heat, and voltage across the Body, Brain, and Nervous System.
* **Part II: Teaching the Machine** (@sec-data, @sec-training, @sec-evaluation) asks what a learned proposer's competence rests on under the second law, endogenous data, when its own actions choose what it observes next.
* **Part III: Running the Machine** (@sec-perception, @sec-memory, @sec-intent, @sec-planning, @sec-enforcement, @sec-placement) builds the runtime around the third law, proposal is not permission.
* **Part IV: Governing the Machine** (@sec-intervention, @sec-verification, @sec-release) applies the fourth law, evidence bounds authority, to decide who may command the machine and under which conditions it may operate.
* **Conclusion** (@sec-frontier) answers the opening question with what the evidence supports.

### For drop-in readers and modular course instructors

Instructors and practitioners often need to study one topic in isolation, such as sensor DMA pipelines, trajectory chunking, or Control Barrier Functions. To support modular use without prerequisite confusion:

* **Orientation at each chapter opening**: Every chapter begins with an orientation section that frames the core problem and states its physical stakes, and the margin stack at each chapter's opening marks the level the chapter works on.
* **Explicit Foundational Context**: Whenever a chapter draws upon a core concept established earlier (such as the proposal boundary, the stopping budget, or the three machine classes), the text provides an immediate inline orientation gloss and a precise section cross-reference.
* **Self-Contained Worked Examples**: Each chapter contains standalone analytical derivations, executable Python calculations, and industrial case studies that can be studied independently.

The margin stack displayed at the start of each chapter is ordered by control rate and physical authority rather than by software dependency alone, establishing the hierarchy from high-frequency motor control up to asynchronous deliberative planning:

```{=latex}
\begin{center}

}
\end{center}
```

### Margin reading aids

The margins carry small, unnumbered visual notes beside the passage where a relationship, a gap in scale, or a threshold is easiest to see. They are reading aids rather than figures to cite, and they come in five forms:

* **Ladders** span orders of magnitude (such as execution rates from inverter switching down to intent-model revision, or sensor ingestion bandwidths).
* **Threshold knees** mark the point beyond which a trend stops holding (such as reflected rotor inertia limiting joint acceleration, force rising with contact stiffness, or tail latency rising with memory bus contention).
* **Budget envelopes** set competing demands against a deadline (such as diffusion denoising times against control periods, or fieldbus cycle budgets).
* **Sequence strips** show multi-phase timing (such as authority handshakes, receding-horizon chunk windows, or the steps that seal a record).
* **Causal chains** trace how a fault propagates and how far it reaches (such as from an unmodeled simulator artifact to a damaged part).

Alongside these visual notes, the margins carry unnumbered **marginal navigation pointers** that trace architectural dependencies across the system stack without interrupting the reading flow of the prose:

* **`↩` Upstream invariant:** Directs the reader back to an earlier chapter where a physical bound, hardware contract, or clock cadence was derived or measured.
* **`↪` Downstream enforcement:** Directs the reader forward to the subsystem that consumes, monitors, or enforces the current concept.
* **`↪` Byte layout / `↪` Protocol:** Jump links that lead directly to machine-readable wire structs and state machines in the systems appendices.
* **`⇄` Structural contrast:** Marks structural contrasts where software abstractions diverge from physical hardware realities.

### The golden thread: An end-to-end forensic trace

To anchor abstract concepts across all seventeen chapters into a cohesive engineering reality, this book weaves a recurring real-world scenario—the **Golden Thread**—through the four parts and the five levels of the machine:

* **Part I · The Physical Challenge (The Plant Hazard)**: An autonomous mobile robot (AMR) navigates an industrial aisle at $v = 1.3\text{ m/s}$. Without warning, an obstacle enters its path with limited clearance. The plant's physical braking capacity, tire-floor Coulomb friction, and actuator response delay dictate a hard stopping budget ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$) that no software optimization can bypass.
* **Part II · The Learning Gap (The Policy Failure)**: The onboard vision-language-action (VLA) policy, trained on nominal demonstrations without sudden intrusions, encounters acute out-of-distribution covariate shift ($\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$). Instead of braking, the generative action chunk decoder proposes an aggressive swerve that violates kinematic turning limits and would destabilize the chassis.
* **Part III · The Runtime Execution (The Silicon Bottleneck)**: Camera exposure, SerDes transport, and neural inference consume critical milliseconds of unguided motion before an action proposal is emitted. When the proposal reaches the shared-memory mailbox, heterogeneous memory bus contention on the system-on-chip threatens the real-time deadline.
* **Part IV · The Safety Shield (The Deterministic Intervention)**: Operating on an isolated real-time safety microcontroller, the high-rate reflex path evaluates the Control Barrier Function ($h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$). Calculating that the proposed swerve will breach the admissible stopping envelope, the quadratic program minimally projects the proposal into an admissible braking clamp, arresting the chassis safely before contact without relying on software optimism.

## Related Books in the Machine Learning Systems Curriculum {#sec-book-series-map .unlisted}

This textbook is part of the *Machine Learning Systems* curriculum. *Introduction to Machine Learning Systems* examines how models use computation and memory on a single machine, focusing on accelerator architectures, memory bandwidth, and tensor runtimes. *Scaling Machine Learning Systems* extends that engineering scope to coordinating distributed training and inference across cluster fleets, focusing on collective communication, parallelization strategies, and fault tolerance.

The curriculum also addresses systems that take autonomous actions. *Agentic Machine Learning Systems* focuses on stateful, goal-directed agent trajectories in digital software environments, where actions invoke software tools, query APIs, or write code within sandboxed environments. *Physical AI Systems* crosses the causal boundary into actions that produce force, motion, and thermodynamic change in the physical world. While digital software environments permit speculative execution, retry loops, and unconstrained error recovery, physical systems operate where mass has momentum, energy dissipates irreversibly, and errors alter reality. Each text offers a complementary perspective, and this book is self-contained, developing the physical, computational, and architectural principles required to engineer dependable embodied machines.
